newsitem.title: UK: LucasVarity profits up despite sterling woes.
newsitem.headline: LucasVarity profits up despite sterling woes.

text.p: Anglo-American engineering giant LucasVarity Plc delivered a bumper 16 percent rise in first-quarter pretax profits Thursday and predicted a year of "modest top-line growth" despite continued pain from the strong British pound.

The manufacturer, whose products range from car components to aerospace, said pretax profits for the first three months to April 30 were line with market forecasts at 72 million pounds ($118 million) against 62 million ($101 million) last year.
"It looks pretty steady as she goes but it does mean numbers are beginning to come through to show that they can do what they said they are going to do," Lehman analyst Charles Armitage said.
Sales were up 8.6 percent to 1.21 billion pounds ($1.98 billion) despite a hit from the strong pound, which wiped 50 million pounds ($82 million) off sales during the period.
LucasVarity Chief Executive Victor Rice was upbeat.
"Against a background of mixed trading conditions and the strength of sterling, the first-quarter results were a creditable start to the year."
Looking ahead, Rice said that despite the currency woes, the first-quarter performance "encourages us to believe that LucasVarity is on track to deliver modest top-line growth this year."
In the first quarter, margins rose to 7.1 percent from 6.9 percent last year.

The figures were based on proforma combined results for the former British Lucas Industries and Varity Corp. of the U.S., which merged in September 1996 to create LucasVarity. The merger created one of the world's top 10 auto component suppliers.

LucasVarity said European and North American automotive markets were expected to be flat for the rest of the year. But "within Europe, the Italian, Spanish and UK markets are expected to outperform last year, while the French market continues to be weak," it said.
The North American light truck sector, where the group has a leading presence, is expected to show continued good growth. Diesel engine markets are seen as mostly robust, as is commercial aerospace.
